questions.question: A supplier offers an all-unit price break: unit price $c_1$ for batches of size $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ for batches with $y\ge q$. Which units of a batch of size $y\ge q$ are bought at price $c_2$?
options: Only the $y-q$ units beyond the threshold $q$.
Every one of the $y$ units in the batch.
Only the unit that reaches the threshold $q$.
Units of later batches, but not of this one.

questions.question: In the classical EOQ model a constant unit price $c$ adds $cD$ to the cost per unit time and is omitted when minimizing. Why must the purchasing cost rate $Dc(y)$ stay in $TCU(y)$ when an all-unit price break at batch size $q$ is offered?
options: Because $Dc(y)$ is always larger than the setup and holding cost rates.
Because $Dc(y)$ is the same for every batch size and must be reported.
Because $Dc(y)$ is charged once per order, like the setup cost $K$.
Because $Dc(y)$ changes with $y$, so it affects which batch is best.

questions.question: In the EOQ model with an all-unit price break, demand rate is $D$, setup cost $K$ per order, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time (the same at both prices), and every unit of a batch of size $y$ costs $c_1$ if $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ if $y\ge q$. Why is $y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}$ the unconstrained minimizer of both price-level cost curves $Dc_1+KD/y+hy/2$ and $Dc_2+KD/y+hy/2$?
options: Because the discount $c_1-c_2$ is too small to move the optimum.
Because the supplier sets the threshold $q$ equal to $y_m$.
Because each curve is one function of $y$ plus a constant $Dc_i$.
Because purchasing cost per unit time is proportional to $y$.

questions.question: In the EOQ model with an all-unit price break, demand rate is $D$, setup cost $K$ per order, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time (the same at both prices), and every unit of a batch of size $y$ costs $c_1$ if $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ if $y\ge q$. A planner argues: '$y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}$ minimizes cost, so ordering a batch $q>y_m$ can never be cheaper.' Why can this argument fail?
options: Because convexity makes cost decrease again for batches above $y_m$.
Because setup plus holding cost per unit time is lower at $q$ than at $y_m$.
Because $y_m$ minimizes only setup plus holding, not purchasing cost.
Because $y_m$ already includes the effect of the unit price $c_1$.

questions.question: A shop has demand $D=200$ units per week, setup cost $K=25$ per order and holding cost $h=1$ per unit per week. Each unit costs 2, or 1.9 if the batch has at least 80 units (all-unit discount). Which batch size is optimal?
options: 100 units, bought at the price 1.9 per unit
80 units, the threshold for the price 1.9
100 units, bought at the price 2 per unit
The cheaper of 100 units and 80 units at price 2

questions.question: Demand is $D=200$ units per week. Units cost $c_1=2$ each for batches of fewer than $q=125$ units and $c_2=1.9$ each for batches of at least 125 units (all-unit discount). By how much does the total cost per week $TCU(y)$ drop as $y$ reaches 125?
options: By 12.5, the saving $q(c_1-c_2)$ on one batch
By 0.1, the price difference $c_1-c_2$ per unit
By 380, the purchasing cost rate $Dc_2$
By 20, the purchasing saving $D(c_1-c_2)$

questions.question: A firm uses $D=50$ units per week and buys in batches of 100 units. Each unit costs 10, or 9 for batches of at least 100 units (all-unit discount). What is the purchasing cost per week?
options: 900, the price of one batch
450, which is $D$ times 9
500, which is $D$ times 10
499.5, at an average price

questions.question: Annual demand is $D=1000$ units, setup cost $K=20$ per order and holding cost $h=4$ per unit per year. Units cost 10 each, or 9.8 each for batches of at least 200 units (all-unit discount). Which batch size gives the lowest total annual cost?
options: 100 units, with full cost 10400 per year
100 units at price 9.8, with full cost 10200
100 or 200 units, since both cost the same
200 units, with full cost 10300 per year

questions.question: Demand is 200 units per week, setup cost 25 per order, holding cost 1 per unit per week, so $\sqrt{2KD/h}=100$. Units cost 2, but 1.9 for orders of more than 120 units, and orders are whole numbers of units. Which batch size is the candidate from the discounted price range?
options: 121 units, the smallest that qualifies
120 units, the stated threshold
100 units, the EOQ at price 1.9
Any size above 120, as all cost the same

questions.question: In the EOQ model with an all-unit price break, demand rate is $D$, setup cost $K$ per order, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time (the same at both prices), and every unit of a batch of size $y$ costs $c_1$ if $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ if $y\ge q$. Suppose $y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}<q$. Why is no batch size larger than $q$ a candidate for the optimum?
options: Above $q$ the purchasing cost rate $Dc_2$ rises with each extra unit.
On $y\ge q$, $Dc_2+KD/y+hy/2$ increases, so $q$ is cheapest there.
Batches larger than $q$ lose the discount again and pay $c_1$.
A larger batch could tie with $q$, but ties are broken towards $q$.

questions.question: In the EOQ model with an all-unit price break, demand rate is $D$, setup cost $K$ per order, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time (the same at both prices), and every unit of a batch of size $y$ costs $c_1$ if $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ if $y\ge q$. Suppose $y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}<q$, and the supplier lowers $c_2$ further while $c_1$, $q$, $K$, $D$ and $h$ stay fixed. How does this change the comparison?
options: $y_m$ rises, because cheaper units justify larger batches.
The discounted candidate moves above $q$ to use the price.
Candidates stay $y_m$ and $q$; only the cost at $q$ falls.
$y_m$ falls, because less money is tied up per batch.

questions.question: In an EOQ model with an all-unit price break, setup cost $K$, demand rate $D$ and fixed holding cost $h$ give $y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}$; batches of at least $q$ units pay $c_2$ per unit, smaller ones $c_1>c_2$. The supplier raises the threshold from $q$ to $q'$, where $y_m<q<q'$. How does the full cost of ordering exactly at the threshold change?
options: It rises, because $KD/y+hy/2$ increases beyond $y_m$.
It is unchanged, because the price $c_2$ is the same at $q$ and $q'$.
It changes only if $c_1$ is changed at the same time.
It falls, because larger batches need fewer orders per unit time.

questions.question: Demand is $D=200$ units per week, setup cost $K=25$ per order and holding cost $h=1$ per unit per week. Units cost 2 each, or 1.9 each for batches of at least 200 units (all-unit discount). What is the total cost per week $TCU(200)$ of ordering 200 units at a time?

In the EOQ model with an all-unit price break, demand rate is $D$, setup cost $K$ per order, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time (the same at both prices), and every unit of a batch of size $y$ costs $c_1$ if $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ if $y\ge q$. A student sets the derivative of $TCU(y)$ to zero, finds $y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}<q$, and stops. Why can this miss the optimum?
options: The derivative is zero at $q$ as well, giving a second stationary point.
$TCU$ is concave beyond $q$, so a zero derivative marks a maximum there.
The derivative of $Dc(y)$ is $c(y)$, which the student left out.
$TCU$ jumps down at $q$; the minimum can sit there with nonzero slope.

questions.question: In the EOQ model with an all-unit price break, demand rate is $D$, setup cost $K$ per order, holding cost $h$ per unit per unit time (the same at both prices), and every unit of a batch of size $y$ costs $c_1$ if $y<q$ and $c_2<c_1$ if $y\ge q$. Let $y_m=\sqrt{2KD/h}$. How is the condition $y_m\ge q$ related to the statement 'ordering $y_m$ units is optimal'?
options: It guarantees $y_m$ is optimal, yet $y_m$ can win without it.
It must hold whenever $y_m$ is optimal, yet gives no guarantee.
It both guarantees that $y_m$ is optimal and is required for it.
It neither guarantees optimality of $y_m$ nor is required for it.

questions.question: Demand is $D=200$ units per week, setup cost $K=25$ per order and holding cost $h=1$ per unit per week, and units cost 2 each. A supplier offers a lower price $2-\delta$ for batches of at least 200 units (all-unit discount). What is the smallest per-unit discount $\delta$ for which ordering 200 units is at least as cheap as ordering the EOQ?
options: $\delta=0.5$
$\delta=25$

questions.question: A product sells at a steady 200 units per week. Each order costs 25 to place, keeping one unit in stock costs 1 per week, and every unit costs 2, or 1.875 when the batch has at least 200 units (all-unit discount). Which batch sizes give the lowest total cost per week of purchasing, ordering and holding?
options: Only 200 units, because the discount beats the EOQ
Exactly two sizes, 100 units and 200 units
Every size from 100 units up to 200 units
Only 100 units, because it is the EOQ
